sections.title: Series Overview and Episode Scope
sections.gist: This episode introduces three foundational agentic design patterns with code examples and live demos, as part of a broader series.

bullets.text: The series teaches how to build agentic solutions ranging from a single agent up to various multi-agent patterns, with each episode providing practical code examples and live demos.

Today's episode covers three patterns — single agent, sequential agent, and parallel agent — while the next episode will cover the orchestrator pattern, review-and-critique with loop agent, and agent-as-tool.

sections.title: Single Agent Pattern
sections.gist: A single agent uses one LLM with tools and a prompt to handle multi-step tasks, but becomes unreliable as complexity grows.

bullets.text: In the single agent pattern, you give one agent a set of tools (e.g., Google Search) and a comprehensive system prompt describing how to accomplish the task; the agent relies on the model's own reasoning to determine the sequence of steps.
The ADK (Agent Development Kit) makes the single agent straightforward to implement in code, and the ADK Web UI allows live testing where tracing confirms the agent uses its tools in a single pass.
When the query is demonstrated live ('plan a trip to San Francisco'), the ADK trace panel shows the agent invoking the search tool and returning a result in one go.

For complex, multi-step requests (e.g., find a late-night sushi restaurant AND find the fastest route), encoding all logic in a single system prompt leads to unreliable behavior because LLMs are non-deterministic and cannot guarantee perfect multi-step adherence every time.

The single agent pattern is simple to implement, easy to debug, and low-latency, making it great for straightforward tasks; its main weakness is lack of control and reliability as task complexity increases.

sections.title: Sequential Agent Pattern
sections.gist: The sequential agent breaks complex tasks into ordered sub-agents that pass results through shared session state, adding control and predictability at the cost of flexibility.

bullets.text: The sequential agent pattern is the first multi-agent pattern and is suited to highly structured, repeatable workflows where order is fixed — the output of one sub-agent becomes the direct input to the next, like an assembly line.

For the trip-planning example, the task is split into two specialized sub-agents — a food-finding agent followed by a transportation agent — guaranteeing the food result is always found before routing is computed.
The ADK Web UI trace confirms sequential execution: the food agent fires first and the transportation agent fires second, with the invocation tree making the order visually explicit.

Sub-agents communicate via a shared session state that acts as a scratchpad — the first agent writes its findings (e.g., the destination restaurant name) and the second agent reads that value using curly-brace placeholders in its system prompt, providing a form of short-term memory.
A live demo shows the food agent finding 'Jin Sho Restaurant Palo Alto', writing it to session state, which is then consumed by the transportation agent to generate directions.
The sequential pattern offers high control and predictability compared to a single agent, but its rigid predefined structure makes it inflexible and unable to adapt to dynamic situations.

sections.title: Parallel Agent Pattern
sections.gist: The parallel agent pattern runs multiple independent specialist agents simultaneously to reduce latency, then combines their results with a sequential aggregator step.

bullets.text: When tasks are independent of each other (e.g., finding a museum, a concert, and a restaurant for one trip), running them sequentially is slow; the parallel agent pattern solves this by launching all specialist agents concurrently.

A common and recommended architecture is to combine parallel and sequential patterns: first run all search agents in parallel, then pass their aggregated session state to a final sequential aggregator agent that synthesizes a single cohesive trip plan.

In ADK, a ParallelAgent is constructed by passing a list of sub-agents (museum_finder_agent, concert_finder_agent, restaurant_finder_agent); each sub-agent writes its result to session state using an output_key parameter.

Each specialist agent (museum finder, restaurant finder) is individually defined with its own tools, instruction, and output_key so its result lands in the correct session state slot for the aggregator to read.
The final ParallelAgent definition combines all three specialists, and the aggregator agent is defined separately to read from session state and generate the unified plan.

The ADK trace for the live demo shows all three sub-agents firing simultaneously, their results accumulating in session state, and then the summarizing agent consuming that state to produce the final output.

The parallel pattern's main benefit is significantly reduced latency for independent subtasks; its drawbacks are higher token/cost usage (multiple agents run simultaneously) and added design complexity from the required gather-and-synthesize step.

sections.title: Recap and Next Episode Preview
sections.gist: A concise comparison of all three patterns covered today closes the episode, with a preview of more advanced patterns coming next.

bullets.text: Single agent is simple and flexible but lacks control; sequential agent adds reliability and control but is inflexible; parallel agent is fast and efficient for independent tasks but increases cost and design complexity.
The next episode will cover three more advanced patterns: the loop-and-critique pattern for self-correction, the coordinator/orchestrator pattern for dynamic routing, and using an agent as a tool.
